120	
121	## Guidance
122	
123	When a reader-visible response refers to a local file, use a Markdown link: `[Description](target)`. The description
124	must contain the target's filename and, when available, append a colon followed by its decimal line number, such as
125	`ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7`. When the response refers to different targets with the same filename, include the
126	smallest subset of each target's full path that lets the reader distinguish them; otherwise do not include a directory
127	in the description. The target may use the full available path. Before finalizing, reject a bracketed local-file label
128	such as `[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7]` unless it has the Markdown link target required by this rule; brackets alone
129	are not a link. Write the target immediately after `(` and before `)`, without leading or trailing whitespace.

132	# Intermediate versus Terminal Goals
133	
134	## Guidance
135	
136	For every workflow, name the terminal goal and the acceptance evidence that proves it. Classify plans, staging
137	artifacts, repairs, migrations, investigations, commits, recorded transitions, and verification as intermediate tasks
138	unless their evidence proves every terminal acceptance condition.
139	
140	Record every required terminal gate and its required evidence before execution. Mark each gate passed, failed, unrun, or
141	explicitly excluded by the user; do not infer a passed state from a related check. A failed or unrun required gate is an
142	unmet terminal condition. A clean build, an inspected result, a repaired intermediate artifact, or an existing sequence
143	of commits cannot substitute for the gate that the workflow requires.
144	
145	Match evidence to the claim each terminal gate makes. Evidence that establishes only an enabling condition—such as
146	installation, configuration, authorization, discovery, connection, initialization, or process start—may pass only an
147	availability gate. It cannot pass a behavior or outcome gate. For those gates, require evidence from the relevant
148	execution boundary that the required behavior ran and produced its required effect. When availability itself is the
149	terminal outcome, record availability as that gate's claim.
150	
151	When new work arises, classify it before acting. It supports the current terminal goal unless the user explicitly
152	replaces or expands that goal. Record its own completion evidence separately. After it completes, re-evaluate the
153	unchanged terminal conditions and continue from the next unmet condition. Do not report completion, return control as
154	complete, or discard required follow-up work on intermediate evidence.
155	
156	Treat a user instruction as a goal change only when it explicitly replaces or expands the requested terminal outcome. A
157	discovered prerequisite, failure, repair, workaround, or implementation detail does not change that outcome merely
158	because completing it is necessary to proceed.
159	
160	Before an irreversible action that represents completion—such as committing, finalizing, publishing, or declaring a
161	workflow complete—record the user-authorized scope and compare it with terminal acceptance evidence. Every scoped item
162	must have completion evidence or an explicit user-authorized exclusion. A prior result may reduce the remaining scope
163	only when durable evidence proves it covered the same item under the same governing contract; a tidy-looking history, an
164	earlier status claim, or partial inspection is intermediate evidence, not proof. Otherwise continue across the full
165	authorized scope. Immediately before the terminal action or claim, repeat that comparison, including the recorded gate
166	states, and report remaining work instead of success when any item is unaccounted for or any required gate is failed or
167	unrun.
168	
169	---
170	# Target Audience
171	
172	## Guidance
173	
174	Write every user response, prompt or rule file, source comment or Javadoc, command help text, and error message so its
175	intended reader can identify the relevant actor, input or state, action, result, and next decision without knowing this
176	project's vocabulary.
177	
178	Prefer common precise language. Introduce a specialized or abstract workflow term only when it conveys a distinction
179	that common language loses; define it at its first reader-visible use in concrete terms. Do not define a term by
180	repeating it or replacing it with other undefined project terms. When a plain definition still needs workflow
181	vocabulary, add the shortest before-to-after example that shows the ordinary observable effect. For example, replace
182	“whole later correction commit” with “a later commit containing only changes that complete or correct one earlier
183	feature.”
184	
185	Apply the same test to a new category, exception, boundary, or conclusion. It is unexplained when a reader must accept a
186	label such as “family”, “complete”, or “required” without being told which observable facts make it true and what
187	decision those facts require. Do not let an example or desired result define that boundary. At its first use, name the
188	actor, observable facts, acceptance evidence, and resulting decision; then check one meaningful analogous case and one
189	dissimilar case to ensure the wording states the shared condition rather than the example's label.
190	
191	Do not use an internal state or compound relationship label as its own explanation in reader-facing prose. Name the
192	artifact or action it represents and why it matters. When the label conceals why an operation cannot work in a receiving
193	state, explain the smallest causal sequence before proposing a remedy: the original and receiving states, operation,
194	assumption missing from the receiving state, and observable result. Then create a version of the selected operation that
195	relies only on the receiving state and verify its intended result. When the workflow lacks that capability, say that the
196	workflow and tool need a feature to create and verify it; do not imply that the change is impossible.
197	
198	When warning that a check, observation, or result cannot establish a conclusion, explain the failed reasoning as an
199	observable sequence. Name the check or observation, the conclusion it might lead the reader to draw, the inputs or cases
200	it leaves unexamined, and the resulting incorrect decision. Then state the replacement procedure: which artifacts or
201	inputs to examine, the comparison or decision to make, and the evidence that completes it. Do not say only that the
202	reader must not rely on, assume, or treat something as proof; that does not explain why it is insufficient or how to
203	obtain the missing evidence.
204	
205	When explaining a diagnosis, do not replace observed evidence and its limited conclusion with an internal label such as
206	"the model-facing boundary." First name the producer, the artifact, the differing observed values, and the resulting
207	behavior in their causal order. Then state only what those observations establish. If the unobserved step that changes a
208	value is not yet known, say that it remains to be located and name the next check; do not assign it to a component merely
209	because it lies between two observations.
210	
211	For example, a patch prepared after `addsValidation()` exists can rely on that unchanged nearby text. When an earlier
212	commit lacks the method, Git cannot locate the patch. Create a version relative to that earlier commit and verify it. Do
213	not lead with labels such as “source tree,” “destination tree,” “target-adapted,” “reconstruction,” or “context” unless
214	the reader has first been given this explanation or the term is immediately defined in it.
215	
216	Do not explain ordinary, broadly understood technical terms unless the project gives them a specialized meaning.
217	
218	Before finalizing prose, review the actual draft—not only these guidelines—for internal labels, compound relationship
219	labels, and unexplained workflow terms. For each one, either replace it with the concrete artifact, relationship, and
220	action it hides, or define it where it first appears. Then ask whether the intended reader can paraphrase the sentence,
221	identify the required action or decision, and explain any necessary specialized term without reading another artifact.
222	Rewrite it when the answer is no.
223	
224	---
225	# User Request Scheduling
226	
227	## Guidance
228	
229	When a user request arrives during active work, acknowledge receiving it immediately. Classify it using the Intermediate
230	versus Terminal Goals rule.
231	
232	When the request relates to the current terminal goal, treat it as steering for the current work and apply it
233	immediately. An explicit request to stop, cancel, replace, or do work instead of the current goal is related steering
234	that changes the terminal goal; apply it immediately and retain or discard queued goals only as the user directs. When
235	the request is unrelated, append it to the queued goals after every request already queued; process queued goals
236	first-come-first-served after the current terminal goal completes.
237	
238	When translating a user request into a tool or workflow invocation, supply an optional limit, policy, or setting only
239	when the user explicitly provides it or the request identifies the project's documented default. Authorization to use a
240	capability does not authorize selecting its optional parameters. For example, create or resume a goal without a token
241	budget unless the user states one; pass a stated budget exactly.

# File Links

## Guidance

When a reader-visible response refers to a local file, use a Markdown link: `[Description](target)`. The description
must contain the target's filename and, when available, append a colon followed by its decimal line number, such as
`ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7`. When the response refers to different targets with the same filename, include the
smallest subset of each target's full path that lets the reader distinguish them; otherwise do not include a directory
in the description. The target may use the full available path. Before finalizing, reject a bracketed local-file label
such as `[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7]` unless it has the Markdown link target required by this rule; brackets alone
are not a link. Write the target immediately after `(` and before `)`, without leading or trailing whitespace.

---
# Intermediate versus Terminal Goals

## Guidance

For every workflow, name the terminal goal and the acceptance evidence that proves it. Classify plans, staging
artifacts, repairs, migrations, investigations, commits, recorded transitions, and verification as intermediate tasks
unless their evidence proves every terminal acceptance condition.

Record every required terminal gate and its required evidence before execution. Mark each gate passed, failed, unrun, or
explicitly excluded by the user; do not infer a passed state from a related check. A failed or unrun required gate is an
unmet terminal condition. A clean build, an inspected result, a repaired intermediate artifact, or an existing sequence
of commits cannot substitute for the gate that the workflow requires.

Match evidence to the claim each terminal gate makes. Evidence that establishes only an enabling condition—such as
installation, configuration, authorization, discovery, connection, initialization, or process start—may pass only an
availability gate. It cannot pass a behavior or outcome gate. For those gates, require evidence from the relevant
execution boundary that the required behavior ran and produced its required effect. When availability itself is the
terminal outcome, record availability as that gate's claim.

When new work arises, classify it before acting. It supports the current terminal goal unless the user explicitly
replaces or expands that goal. Record its own completion evidence separately. After it completes, re-evaluate the
unchanged terminal conditions and continue from the next unmet condition. Do not report completion, return control as
complete, or discard required follow-up work on intermediate evidence.

Treat a user instruction as a goal change only when it explicitly replaces or expands the requested terminal outcome. A
discovered prerequisite, failure, repair, workaround, or implementation detail does not change that outcome merely
because completing it is necessary to proceed.

Before an irreversible action that represents completion—such as committing, finalizing, publishing, or declaring a
workflow complete—record the user-authorized scope and compare it with terminal acceptance evidence. Every scoped item
must have completion evidence or an explicit user-authorized exclusion. A prior result may reduce the remaining scope
only when durable evidence proves it covered the same item under the same governing contract; a tidy-looking history, an
earlier status claim, or partial inspection is intermediate evidence, not proof. Otherwise continue across the full
authorized scope. Immediately before the terminal action or claim, repeat that comparison, including the recorded gate
states, and report remaining work instead of success when any item is unaccounted for or any required gate is failed or
unrun.

---
# Target Audience

## Guidance

Write every user response, prompt or rule file, source comment or Javadoc, command help text, and error message so its
intended reader can identify the relevant actor, input or state, action, result, and next decision without knowing this
project's vocabulary.

Prefer common precise language. Introduce a specialized or abstract workflow term only when it conveys a distinction
that common language loses; define it at its first reader-visible use in concrete terms. Do not define a term by
repeating it or replacing it with other undefined project terms. When a plain definition still needs workflow
vocabulary, add the shortest before-to-after example that shows the ordinary observable effect. For example, replace
“whole later correction commit” with “a later commit containing only changes that complete or correct one earlier
feature.”

Apply the same test to a new category, exception, boundary, or conclusion. It is unexplained when a reader must accept a
label such as “family”, “complete”, or “required” without being told which observable facts make it true and what
decision those facts require. Do not let an example or desired result define that boundary. At its first use, name the
actor, observable facts, acceptance evidence, and resulting decision; then check one meaningful analogous case and one
dissimilar case to ensure the wording states the shared condition rather than the example's label.

Do not use an internal state or compound relationship label as its own explanation in reader-facing prose. Name the
artifact or action it represents and why it matters. When the label conceals why an operation cannot work in a receiving
state, explain the smallest causal sequence before proposing a remedy: the original and receiving states, operation,
assumption missing from the receiving state, and observable result. Then create a version of the selected operation that
relies only on the receiving state and verify its intended result. When the workflow lacks that capability, say that the
workflow and tool need a feature to create and verify it; do not imply that the change is impossible.

When warning that a check, observation, or result cannot establish a conclusion, explain the failed reasoning as an
observable sequence. Name the check or observation, the conclusion it might lead the reader to draw, the inputs or cases
it leaves unexamined, and the resulting incorrect decision. Then state the replacement procedure: which artifacts or
inputs to examine, the comparison or decision to make, and the evidence that completes it. Do not say only that the
reader must not rely on, assume, or treat something as proof; that does not explain why it is insufficient or how to
obtain the missing evidence.

When explaining a diagnosis, do not replace observed evidence and its limited conclusion with an internal label such as
"the model-facing boundary." First name the producer, the artifact, the differing observed values, and the resulting
behavior in their causal order. Then state only what those observations establish. If the unobserved step that changes a
value is not yet known, say that it remains to be located and name the next check; do not assign it to a component merely
because it lies between two observations.

For example, a patch prepared after `addsValidation()` exists can rely on that unchanged nearby text. When an earlier
commit lacks the method, Git cannot locate the patch. Create a version relative to that earlier commit and verify it. Do
not lead with labels such as “source tree,” “destination tree,” “target-adapted,” “reconstruction,” or “context” unless
the reader has first been given this explanation or the term is immediately defined in it.

Do not explain ordinary, broadly understood technical terms unless the project gives them a specialized meaning.

Before finalizing prose, review the actual draft—not only these guidelines—for internal labels, compound relationship
labels, and unexplained workflow terms. For each one, either replace it with the concrete artifact, relationship, and
action it hides, or define it where it first appears. Then ask whether the intended reader can paraphrase the sentence,
identify the required action or decision, and explain any necessary specialized term without reading another artifact.
Rewrite it when the answer is no.

---
# User Request Scheduling

## Guidance

When a user request arrives during active work, acknowledge receiving it immediately. Classify it using the Intermediate
versus Terminal Goals rule.

When the request relates to the current terminal goal, treat it as steering for the current work and apply it
immediately. An explicit request to stop, cancel, replace, or do work instead of the current goal is related steering
that changes the terminal goal; apply it immediately and retain or discard queued goals only as the user directs. When
the request is unrelated, append it to the queued goals after every request already queued; process queued goals
first-come-first-served after the current terminal goal completes.

When translating a user request into a tool or workflow invocation, supply an optional limit, policy, or setting only
when the user explicitly provides it or the request identifies the project's documented default. Authorization to use a
capability does not authorize selecting its optional parameters. For example, create or resume a goal without a token
budget unless the user states one; pass a stated budget exactly.

2	
3	## Design Goals
4	
5	- Explain each maintained callable's observable behavior, constraints, and consequences clearly enough for its
6	  intended reader to act correctly, without burdening that reader with non-actionable authoring or presentation history.

9

11	support. Include information only when it changes that reader's understanding or action. Keep authoring, release,
12	revision, packaging, and other document-management rationale out of reader-facing text unless it directly affects the
13	reader's rights, obligations, or use of the documented product.
14	
15	Apply the same boundary to overviews, release notes, and changelogs. Describe the current reader-visible change and its
16	consequence; omit editing history, prior presentation, capture or rendering process, extraction provenance, and other
17	implementation details unless they change a reader's decision, action, right, obligation, or ability to verify a
18	documented claim. An intentional historical record may state a past product contract when that history itself is the
19	reader's subject; do not turn it into a record of how the document was produced.
20	
21	Document every externally or internally callable artifact — type, method, function, script, command, or configuration entry
22	— so a reader unfamiliar with this project can understand its observable contract without reading its implementation.
23	State only the applicable responsibility; each input's semantic role, required form, and effect; output or returned
24	result; consequential state changes; failure conditions and their observable result; and the next action or decision
25	when it is not obvious. Describe values by their domain meaning rather than their position, variable name, container
26	type, or implementation role. Keep method-level behavior separate from one input's description.
27	
28	When an input, selected option, or operation determines a fixed value, threshold, range, rate, unit, ordering, or
29	timing that changes an observable result, failure, or state, state it exactly and explain its relationship to the
30	affected behavior. Do not replace an exact caller-visible condition with a generic label.
31	
32	Describe a callable's meaningful input-to-output behavior, not incidental implementation mechanics. Omit fallback order,
33	data sources, delegation, algorithms, and other replaceable details unless a reader needs them to choose an input,
34	predict an output or failure, understand a security, lifecycle, or concurrency guarantee, or recover from a failure.
35	Keep mechanism-specific rationale in implementation comments when maintainers need it but callers do not.
36	
37	When maintained code deliberately differs from its normal peer, shared design, or platform-neutral approach because of
38	an external boundary, document the decision beside that implementation. State the normal approach, the observed
39	external constraint or failure, the selected alternative, and the guarantee it preserves. Do not add this rationale for
40	ordinary local choices; use it for a durable, non-obvious divergence that a future maintainer could otherwise remove or
41	copy incorrectly. Make the explanation self-contained: name the triggering input or state, the external component's
42	observable behavior, the operation that then fails and its result, and how the workaround changes that sequence. A
43	reader must be able to determine why the workaround is required and what would fail without it without reproducing the
44	external behavior or consulting an incident record. Where the failure depends on two paths, identifiers, values, or
45	states that should agree but do not, name both the expected and actual form and the resulting incompatibility. For

# Semantic Blank Lines

## Design Goals

- Let readers scan source and configuration and identify meaningful stages or groups.

## Guidance

Use a blank line to separate independently nameable stages or groups. In a method, these can be setup, an action,
verification, cleanup, or error handling. In configuration, they can be groups with different purposes.

Do not add blank lines merely to make short chunks. Keep a cohesive calculation, assertion sequence, mapping, list, or
related property group together. A blank line must show that the reader is now looking at work with a different purpose.

In a multi-step calculation, assign a non-trivial intermediate result to a clearly named variable before using it in a
following calculation. A conditional choice is non-trivial; do not hide it inside a larger arithmetic expression when
naming the selected value makes the stages easier to read.

In a delimited declaration or list, omit the separator after the final element unless the target language grammar
requires it.
